title: No public shame (Avot 3:11)
hookLine: Elazar of Modi'in: shaming someone in public costs a person dearly
tomorrow: how do you greet someone you'd rather avoid?

lines: WHOEVER SHAMES HIS FELLOW IN PUBLIC.
cards: A speech, a microphone, a room full of friends, and one perfect joke at somebody's expense. Everyone laughs. One face goes pale.
What costs more than money and takes one sentence? Rabbi Elazar of Modi'in lists grave things in Avot, and one of them is this: whoever shames his fellow in public.
Even with Torah and good deeds, he says, that person has lost something no deed easily buys back.

teach.b: The Hebrew is vivid: malbin p'nei chavero, whitening his fellow's face. The Talmud takes the picture literally. The red drains out and the white comes in, so shaming someone in public is like shedding blood.
And it tells of Tamar, who, as she was being led out to be punished, would not name Judah in front of everyone; she sent him his own things privately and let him decide.
Some sages draw the lesson that it's better to suffer than to shame someone in public. That's the day's word, lightly: no public shame.
And it gathers the week. You and yours are His, so the person in front of you is His too. The tree is Torah too, and so is the face of the one you're about to joke about.
Review: say it once more, and gentler.
Deeds first: the kind act beats the clever line. Pleasant to people: let them rest around you. Don't waste the day on a laugh that costs someone their color.

how: Jewish ethics treats public embarrassment as a grave wrong; correction is meant to be private and gentle, and some communities give help to those in need discreetly so no one is shamed.

o: never let anyone see you make a mistake
never humiliate anyone in front of others
never admit your own faults in public

games.q: the face and the week — tap the pairs.
p: would not name Judah in public
the person in front of you too

s: the Talmud compares shaming someone in public to shedding blood
the red drains from the face, and the white comes in.
Avot 3:11 says public shaming is minor if you're otherwise a good person
even with Torah and good deeds, it says, the loss is grave.
a joke at someone's expense can't count as public shame
the test is the pale face, not the speaker's intent.

games.q: in a team meeting, a colleague's mistake is about to go up on the big screen in front of everyone. what does Avot 3:11 point to?
o: raise it with the colleague privately first.
show it; honesty means everyone should see.
say nothing ever; mistakes don't really matter.
games.why: Tamar sent Judah his things privately rather than shame him in public. the mistake can still be fixed; the face doesn't have to go white.

practice: Bring to mind someone who's been the joke of the room lately, at work, at school, in a family chat. See the next time it starts, and find one plain sentence that would turn it gently, like, let's give them a break.
Say that sentence once, under your breath, so it's ready.

wordCard.voice: No public shame: Elazar of Modi'in's warning, and the Talmud's picture of a face going white as the blood drains.

orig.note: Hebrew: one who whitens his fellow's face in public, Avot 3:11.

carryVoice: Your line: no public shame. Let every face in the room keep its own color. Two weeks, done.

sources.ref: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:11 (Rabbi Elazar of Modi'in)
Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 58b–59a (whitening a face is like shedding blood; better to be cast into a furnace than shame another in public, from Tamar)
